title: WebSocket connection lifecycle
description: Project: WebSocket connection lifecycle. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: A WebSocket connection is not a single event; it is a lifecycle with opening, open, message, close, and error phases. Senior engineers treat each phase as an opportunity to observe, recover, and optimize. Understanding the lifecycle helps you debug dropped connections, handle scaling correctly, and provide a reliable user experience across flaky mobile networks.

items: HTTP upgrade handshake: client sends Upgrade: websocket, server responds with 101 Switching Protocols
Opening phase: authentication, rate limiting, and subscription setup happen before the connection is usable
Active phase: heartbeats keep the connection alive; message handlers process inbound frames
Close phase: application-initiated close versus network-driven close; normal closure versus abnormal drop
Error phase: onerror fires when the transport breaks; reconnect logic must avoid stampedes
Reconnection strategies: exponential backoff with jitter, max delay caps, and circuit breakers
Scaling consideration: stateless connection managers require a shared message bus to fan out messages

terms.definition: The HTTP exchange that transitions a normal HTTP connection into a WebSocket connection using the Upgrade and Connection headers.
The HTTP status code indicating the server has accepted the protocol upgrade.
A pattern that stops retry attempts after repeated failures, allowing the system to recover and preventing resource exhaustion.
When many clients reconnect simultaneously after an outage, overwhelming the server with a spike of connection requests.
Randomized delay added to backoff intervals to prevent synchronized retries across many clients.

data.text: WebSocket bugs are some of the hardest to reproduce because they depend on network conditions, load balancer timeouts, and mobile carrier NAT behavior. A senior engineer who understands the lifecycle can design reconnection logic that recovers gracefully and adds observability at every phase so issues are caught before users notice.

data.title: Implement heartbeats early
data.text: Send a ping every thirty seconds and expect a pong within five seconds. If no pong arrives, close the socket and trigger the reconnection flow. Heartbeats detect half-open connections caused by firewalls or mobile NATs that silently drop TCP state.

items: Immediate retry: only for the first attempt; avoids unnecessary delay on transient drops
Exponential backoff: double the delay after each failure up to a maximum
Jitter: add a random fraction of the backoff delay to spread reconnections over time
Circuit breaker: after five failures in ten seconds, pause reconnections for thirty seconds
Back-off reset: once a connection succeeds, reset all failure counters and backoff state

data.caption: WebSocket connection lifecycle with reconnection flow
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Client] --> B[HTTP Upgrade]
    B -->|101| C[OPEN]
    B -->|Error| D[Reconnect]
    C --> E{Message received?}
    E -->|Yes| F[Process message]
    E -->|No| G{Heartbeat timeout?}
    G -->|Yes| D
    G -->|No| E
    F --> H{Server close?}
    H -->|Yes| I[ONCLOSE]
    H -->|No| E
    I --> D
    D --> J{Backoff maxed?}
    J -->|No| K[Wait + jitter]
    K --> B
    J -->|Yes| L[Show offline UI]

items: Authenticate during the upgrade request using a JWT or session cookie before accepting the WebSocket
Assign each connection a unique ID and store it in a connection registry mapped to user ID and room IDs
Track connection metadata: IP address, user agent, connected at timestamp, last heartbeat timestamp
Use a pub/sub system like Redis to broadcast messages across multiple server instances without tight coupling
Gracefully close idle connections after a server-side timeout and emit a close event with code 1001 Going Away

cards.title: 1000 Normal Closure
cards.description: The connection closed successfully after the endpoint completed its work.

cards.title: 1001 Going Away
cards.description: The endpoint is going away, such as a server restart or browser navigation away.

cards.title: 1006 Abnormal Closure
cards.description: The connection closed without a close frame, usually due to network loss.
cons: Client cannot distinguish server restart from network glitch

data.title: Implement a WebSocket client wrapper
data.description: Write a TypeScript WebSocket client class that manages the full lifecycle: connection, heartbeats, message queuing while offline, exponential backoff reconnection with jitter, and a circuit breaker after repeated failures.
steps: Create a class that wraps the native WebSocket API
Implement a heartbeat sender that pings every thirty seconds
Implement a reconnection method with exponential backoff and jitter
Queue messages sent while the socket is disconnected and flush them on reconnect
Add event listeners for open, message, error, and close
Expose a ready state observable so UI components can show connection status
data.expectedOutcome: You should have a reusable client that survives network drops without losing messages or hammering the server with retries.

items.question: Should I reconnect immediately after a close event?
items.answer: No. Use exponential backoff with jitter. Immediate retries cause a thundering herd when the server recovers, which can extend the outage.

items.question: How do I know if the server is down versus a network issue?
items.answer: You cannot distinguish them reliably from the client. Use a circuit breaker: if reconnection fails repeatedly, assume the server is unavailable and show an offline UI rather than retrying indefinitely.

items.question: Do I need sticky sessions with WebSocket?
items.answer: Not if you use a pub/sub message bus like Redis. Each server instance manages its own connections and publishes messages to the bus, which delivers them to the correct instance. Sticky sessions are a fallback for simple setups.

data.title: Summary
points: Treat WebSocket as a lifecycle, not a single connection
Add heartbeats and reconnection logic from the start
Use backoff with jitter to prevent stampedes
Observe every phase with metrics so debugging is possible in production
data.takeaway: A senior engineer designs the connection lifecycle for failure, because failure is the most common state in distributed systems.
